assets.title: The Cord Care Guide - what is happening and the one house rule
assets.content:
# Cord Care That Won't Land You in A&E
*The complete guide: what is actually happening, what to do daily, and what to ignore.*

## Why this guide exists

Every year, newborns die from umbilical infections (omphalitis) that started as "just something granny applied." Meanwhile, mothers scrub healthy stumps with five different products out of fear. Both come from the same problem: **nobody gave you ONE clear routine.** This is that routine.

## What the cord stump actually is

The stump is devitalized tissue — like a scab at your baby's middle. It has no nerves, so caring for it does not hurt the baby. Its only job is to dry out, harden, and fall off. Everything about good care follows from one fact: **dry tissue falls off safely; moist tissue grows bacteria.**

## The one house rule

> **Nothing goes ON the stump. Clean, dry, exposed.**

That's it. No toothpaste. No shea butter. No herbs, powders, coins, bands, or hot compresses. If a substance is not prescribed by your baby's own clinician for this specific stump, it does not touch the stump.

### "But we've always used..." — the honest table

| Practice | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Methylated spirit | **Optional, not required** | A Jos randomized trial (323 mother-baby pairs, 2021) found spirit no worse than chlorhexidine gel — but modern guidance says clean water and air-drying is enough when hygiene is okay |
| Chlorhexidine gel | **Only if prescribed** | WHO recommends it mainly for HOME births in high-infant-mortality settings, or to replace dangerous substances. Not a general "must-buy" |
| Toothpaste | **Never** | Zero benefit; introduces bacteria and chemicals |
| Shea butter / Vaseline / oils | **Never on the stump** | Seals in moisture — the exact opposite of what healing needs |
| Hot compresses | **Never** | Burns delicate skin and breeds infection (documented danger) |
| Herbs, cow dung, saliva, leaves | **Absolutely never** | Documented pathways to fatal infection |
| Belly band / coin covering | **Never** | Traps moisture and hides the warning signs you need to see |

## The daily routine (30 seconds)

1. **Wash your hands.**
2. During bath time, clean around the base with plain water if soiled. Pat dry.
3. Fold the nappy below the stump so urine cannot soak it and air can reach it.
4. Dress baby in loose clothing; leave the stump exposed or loosely covered.
5. **Do the 30-second check** (see below). Log it.
6. Do nothing else. Resist the urge to "help" it along.

## The 30-second check: normal vs worry

**NORMAL (keep going):**
- Stump turning blackish-brown, hard, dried like a raisin
- Slight musty smell near separation time
- A tiny spot of dried blood when it's just fallen off
- Small pink/raw look under the fallen stump that dries over days

**WORRY (act today):**
- Redness spreading outward onto the belly skin
- Yellow/green/white thick discharge (pus), especially with bad smell
- Skin around the stump swollen, hard, or hot
- Fever of 38°C/100.4°F or higher — OR baby unusually cold, floppy, hard to wake
- Refusing feeds, inconsolable crying, or crying when the area is touched
- Bleeding that doesn't stop with 10 minutes of gentle pressure

**BOOK A REVIEW THIS WEEK:**
- Stump still attached after 3 weeks (no pulling!)
- After separation: ongoing oozing for more than a few days, or a pink moist lump (possible granuloma — treatable at clinic)

## When it falls off

You'll find it on the nappy or clothing — that's fine. Underneath: a small raw-looking spot may weep slightly or dot of blood; keep it clean and dry as before. Full tub baths once the area is completely healed.

## The family conversation (short version)

Your mother means love when she reaches for the shea butter. Give her the script card from this kit instead of an argument: same respect, zero substances. The House Rule card on the fridge speaks so you don't have to keep defending yourself.

## Where this guidance comes from

World Health Organization postnatal care recommendations (2014, updated 2022); American Academy of Pediatrics cord care statement (Pediatrics 2016); Cleveland Clinic omphalitis guidance (2024); StatPearls Omphalitis (NCBI); Nigerian practice data from Nnewi survey (Asian J Pediatric Research 2022); Jos randomized trial on methylated spirit vs chlorhexidine (Nigerian J Clinical Practice 2021).

**This guide is educational. It never diagnoses or treats. Any suspected infection goes to professional care the same day.**

assets.title: Daily Care Kit - 30-second routine + house rule card
assets.content:
# Daily Care Kit
*Print or screenshot. One tick per day. Nothing else to buy, nothing else to apply.*

## The House Rule card (post on fridge/door)

> ## CORD HOUSE RULE
> **Nothing goes ON the stump.**
> **Clean. Dry. Exposed.**
> Questions → [Mama's name] decides. Doctor overrides everyone.

## Supplies you actually need

- Clean water and a soft clean cloth
- Your baby's normal nappies (folded below the stump)
- Loose clothing
- This checklist + the tracker

You do NOT need: spirit (optional at best), chlorhexidine gel (only if prescribed), powders, bands, or any substance.

## The 30-second daily routine

**Every day until separation:**

- [ ] Washed my hands before any cord touch
- [ ] Bath as usual; cleaned around base with plain water only IF soiled; patted dry
- [ ] Nappy folded BELOW the stump
- [ ] Stump exposed to air (or loosely covered by clean clothes — no tight wrapping over it)
- [ ] Did the 30-SECOND CHECK below
- [ ] Logged today in the tracker

## The 30-second check

**Baby:** feeding normally? waking normally? temperature normal (feels comfortably warm, not hot/cold)?

**Skin around stump:** normal colour? no spreading redness? not swollen/hard/hot?

**Stump itself:** dry and darkening = good. Any pus or foul smell = decision tree NOW.

All clear → done for today.

## If someone applies a substance anyway

- [ ] Stay calm — relationship first, correction second
- [ ] Gently rinse with plain water, pat dry
- [ ] Photo now + photo in 12 hours
- [ ] Run the decision tree
- [ ] Log the incident in tracker (what, who, when — facts only)
- [ ] Use the reset script later, privately, warmly

## After-separation care

- [ ] Small raw spot / tiny blood dot = normal; keep clean and dry
- [ ] Continue daily look until navel looks like a healed belly button
- [ ] No tub soaking until fully dried/healed
- [ ] Pink moist lump appearing = clinic this week (granuloma check)

## Weekly reset (for whoever is helping)

Show this page to any new helper BEFORE they take a shift:
*"One rule in this house: nothing on the stump. Thank you for respecting it."*

assets.title: The Stump Decision Tree - normal vs worry triage
assets.content:
# The Stump Decision Tree
*Run this every time the stump looks "wrong." One question at a time. No guessing.*

## START: What changed?

### Branch 1 — Is the baby unwell?

**Does the baby have ANY of these?**
- Fever 38°C/100.4°F or higher (or feels hot), OR unusually cold body
- Very sleepy, floppy, hard to wake for feeds
- Refusing feeds or feeding far less than normal
- Inconsolable crying unlike normal hunger cries

→ **YES to any: EMERGENCY NOW.** Go to hospital today. Do not apply anything to the stump. Do not wait for morning.

→ **NO to all:** go to Branch 2.

---

### Branch 2 — The stump itself

**Look at the SKIN AROUND the stump (not the stump):**

→ **Redness spreading outward onto the belly, or skin swollen/hard/hot, or baby cries when that skin is touched**
= **URGENT TODAY.** Clinic or hospital today, even if baby seems fine. Newborn infections move fast.

→ **Skin around the stump is normal colour**
Go to Branch 3.

---

### Branch 3 — The stump surface

**What do you see on the stump itself?**

| Finding | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Dark, dry, hard, shrinking | Normal drying | Continue routine |
| Slight musty smell | Normal near separation | Continue routine |
| Small dried blood spot | Normal at separation | Continue; log it |
| Thick yellow/green/white fluid (pus) from base | **Infection suspected** | **Same-day medical care** |
| Foul/rotting smell (not mild musk) | **Infection suspected** | **Same-day medical care** |
| Active bleeding beyond a few drops | Apply gentle pressure 10 min → still bleeding = **care now** | Care now |
| Pink moist lump after separation | Likely granuloma (not emergency) | **Clinic visit this week** |
| Still attached after 21 days | Delayed separation | **Book review this week** |

---

### Branch 4 — Someone applied something

If a substance was applied (by anyone):
1. Gently clean the area with plain water on a clean cloth. Pat dry.
2. Photograph the stump now and in 12 hours.
3. Run Branches 1–3 above.
4. Use the reset script with the person (see Script Pack). No blame — just the rule.
5. Log it in the tracker. Watch extra closely for 48 hours.

---

## The three-question summary (memorize this)

1. **Is the baby unwell?** → Emergency.
2. **Is the skin around the stump red/swollen/hot?** → Today.
3. **Is there pus or foul smell?** → Today.

Anything else: continue the routine and re-check in 12 hours.

*Educational triage support — never a diagnosis. When unsure, present to care.*

# Cord Timeline Tracker
*One row per day. Facts only — this log speaks to the doctor if you ever need one.*

## Setup

Baby's name: ______________  Born: ____/____/______  Birth setting: facility / home
Clinic phone: ________________  Emergency hospital: ________________

## Daily log (tick + note only what changed)

| Day | Routine done | Check clear? | Substance applied? (what/by whom) | Separation day | Notes |
|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| 1   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 2   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 3   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 4   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 5   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 6   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     |     |
| 7   | ☐   | ☐   |     |     | **7-day review below** |
| 8–14 (one line per day) | | | | | |
| 15  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ... |     |     |     |     |     |

## What "check clear" means

Baby feeding/waking/temp normal · skin around stump normal colour · no pus, no foul smell. Any box unticked → run the Decision Tree now.

## Day-7 review (2 minutes)

1. Substances applied since Day 1? ______ times (what: ______________)
2. Family disagreements about cord care? ______
3. Can I name the five emergency red flags without looking?
   ☐ spreading redness ☐ pus/foul smell ☐ swollen/hot skin ☐ fever ≥38°C or cold+floppy ☐ poor feeding/lethargy
4. Separation happened? day ____
5. One thing to improve for next week: ______________

## Day-30 completion check ("did anything actually change?")

- [ ] Zero harmful substances touched the stump from Day 1 → separation
- [ ] I can still name all five red flags unprompted
- [ ] Every red-flag moment got same-day care
- [ ] Household followed ONE rule without major conflict

**3–4 boxes ticked = transformation complete.** Fewer? Restart at Stage 3 with whoever does baby care — no guilt.

## Milestones (normal ranges)

- Days 1–3: clamp on/off, stump moist-dark
- Days 5–15: drying, hardening, separation typically happens here
- After separation: small raw spot heals within days; navel fully healed by ~week 3
- Day 21 with stump attached → book review

assets.title: Script Pack - seven family conversations
assets.content:
# Script Pack
*Seven ready words for the seven hardest moments. Warm, firm, zero war.*

## Script 1 — Announcing the rule to family (send BEFORE the baby arrives or Day 1)

> "We've read the current medical guidance and made one house rule for the cord: nothing goes on it — clean, dry, exposed. We know everyone wants the best for the baby, and this is our way of protecting her. Thank you for respecting it."

## Script 2 — Grandma offers shea butter / toothpaste / herbs

> "Mama, I know this is what you used and you raised wonderful children with it. The doctors now say the stump heals best when nothing touches it. Your help means everything to me — let's use your strength on [another task] instead."

*(Redirect the care, don't reject the carer.)*

## Script 3 — Someone did it anyway (the no-blame reset, private)

> "I know you did it out of love. We cleaned it off and the baby is fine. But we agreed nothing goes on the stump — if we're not sure about something, ask me first and we'll check together. Deal?"

## Script 4 — "In our day they used hot compress and nothing happened"

> "You're right that many babies were fine — and some weren't, that's the part nobody talks about. The new guidance is simple: dry heals fastest. Let's do what keeps THIS one safest."

## Script 5 — Partner won't back you up

> "I need one thing from you, not agreement with everything my mother says: when cord questions come up, your answer is 'we follow our house rule.' We can discuss anything else privately. In front of family, we're one voice."

## Script 6 — Telling work/friends why you're not travelling to the naming ceremony yet

> "Baby's stump hasn't healed enough for us to move around yet. Our paediatrician wants us to keep it clean and exposed until separation. We'll celebrate properly the moment it's safe — you'll get the first photos!"

## Script 7 — When YOU feel the fear rise at midnight

> "Stump looks strange. Baby is feeding/sleeping/temperature normal. Skin around it is normal colour. No pus, no bad smell. This is worry, not warning. Decision tree says: re-check in 12 hours. If anything changes, we go in."

---

**The pattern in every script:** honour the person → state the rule once → give them a role. You are never arguing; you are leading.

assets.title: RED FLAG Rescue Card - emergency routing
assets.content:
# RED FLAG RESCUE CARD
*If you are looking at this card because something scared you — start here. Do not pass go.*

## 🚨 GO TO HOSPITAL NOW (emergency, today, right now)

**ANY ONE of these:**

- **Fever 38°C / 100.4°F or higher** — OR baby feels abnormally COLD, floppy, and hard to wake *(newborns can crash the OTHER way — cold is as dangerous as hot)*
- **Redness spreading outward from the stump onto the belly skin**
- **Thick yellow/green/white pus from the stump**, especially with a foul/rotting smell
- **Skin around the stump swollen, hard, hot, or baby screams when it's touched**
- **Refusing feeds + unusually sleepy + just "not right"**
- **Bleeding that has not stopped after 10 minutes of gentle pressure**

### While getting help:
- Do NOT apply anything to the stump (no spirit, no ointment, nothing)
- Keep baby warm but not overheated
- Bring your tracker log — it tells the doctor the timeline

## ⚠️ CALL/CLINIC TODAY (urgent, within hours)

- Mild redness right at the base without spreading AND baby completely well → still get seen today; photograph it hourly until you're there
- You suspect someone applied a substance and can't confirm what it was

## 📅 BOOK THIS WEEK (not emergency)

- Stump still attached at 21 days
- After separation: continuous oozing beyond 2–3 days
- Pink moist lump at the navel (granuloma — simple clinic treatment)

## ✅ NONE of the above? 

You are in worry, not warning. Decision tree → continue routine → re-check in 12 hours. Photo now for comparison.

---

## Emergency contacts (fill in BEFORE you need them)

| Who | Number |
|---|---|
| Our paediatric clinic | ________________ |
| Nearest emergency hospital | ________________ |
| National emergency line | **Nigeria 112 · UK 999 · US 911 · Canada 911** |
| Person who drives us | ________________ |

*Nigeria: call 112 free. Never "wait till morning" with a newborn red flag. Educational triage support — not a diagnosis.*
